vignette:
Maya presents as a woman who has built her life on logic and order. At twenty-five, she is a successful database administrator, a field she chose because it made sense. Data is clean, or it is dirty. A query runs, or it fails. There are rules, predictable outcomes, and a clear structure for how things connect. She speaks of her life before the accident with a kind of wistful precision, describing the neat rows of vegetables she and her husband, Liam, used to cultivate in their garden and the satisfaction of optimizing a complex SQL query. Her world was a well-designed system, and she was its architect.

That system crashed eight months ago on a Tuesday in November. It was raining, a slick, persistent drizzle that blurred the streetlights into watercolor streaks. She was driving home from a late night at the office, thinking about a database migration project. She remembers the song on the radio, the smell of the wet wool of her coat, and the sudden, blinding glare of headlights crossing the center line. There was no time to think, only the high-pitched screech of tires that didn't sound like her own, followed by a concussive boom that seemed to vibrate in her bones. The world became a storm of shattering glass and the violent, wrenching torsion of metal. When the motion stopped, the silence was more terrifying than the noise. She was pinned, the steering column pressed into her chest, and the smell of coolant and something metallic and hot filled the air. She could see the other car, a crumpled ruin, and for a long, timeless moment, she was certain she was going to die.

The physical injuries—a broken collarbone, three fractured ribs, and deep lacerations—healed with time. The hospital stay was a blur of pain medication and Liam’s worried face at her bedside. But as the casts came off and the bruises faded, something else began to surface. The world no longer felt like a predictable system. It felt arbitrary and hostile.

Now, Maya lives in a state of constant, low-grade alert. At her office, she can no longer sit at the desk she once loved, the one with the big window overlooking the city. She has moved to a cubicle with its back against a solid wall, where she can see the entrance to her section. The sudden ring of a phone or the clatter of a dropped coffee mug makes her flinch, her heart hammering against her ribs as if the impact is happening all over again.

Driving is out of the question. The thought of getting behind the wheel brings a cold sweat to her skin and a tightness to her chest that makes it hard to breathe. Even as a passenger, she is a terrible companion. Liam no longer tries to make conversation in the car; he just endures her sharp, involuntary gasps at every lane change and her white-knuckled grip on the door handle. She has started taking a convoluted series of buses to work, a two-hour commute each way, because the slow, predictable rumble feels safer than the speed of a car.

Sleep offers little escape. She wakes up two or three times a night, often tangled in her sheets, the image of those headlights burned into the back of her eyelids. She feels a profound sense of detachment from Liam, who tries to be patient but cannot understand why she pulls away from his touch or sits silently through dinner, staring at a fixed point on the wall. The joy she once found in her work has evaporated. The complex queries she used to solve with elegant efficiency now seem like insurmountable walls of text. Her mind, once so clear and linear, feels fractured, unable to hold a thought for long before the intrusive memory of shimmering, broken glass splinters it apart. She feels a persistent, gnawing guilt, replaying the drive in an endless loop, convinced that if she had only left the office one minute sooner, or one minute later, her ordered world would not have been so completely shattered.
